What should a Spokane seller know about the local housing picture?

Spokane homeowners hold a median home value of $363,500, and 58.8 percent of households own the place they live, according to the Census Bureau's 2020-2024 estimates. The city had an estimated 230,783 residents on July 1, 2025, up 0.8 percent from the April 2020 base.

Spokane sits on the Spokane River in eastern Washington at 1,843 feet above sea level, about 18 miles from the Idaho border and 229 miles east of Seattle. The city covers 60.02 square miles. A citywide median says little about one block, so compare against recent sales on your own street.

How do the 2026 wildfires affect selling a house in Spokane?

They matter a great deal if your house or street was touched. In early August 2026 the Old Trails Fire destroyed more than 600 buildings, which the encyclopedia entry for Spokane calls the worst disaster in the city's history, and the City of Spokane has since run a recovery program for burned and damaged properties.

The city's wildfire information page and the county's recovery pages point owners to several resources:

  • Owners of properties hit by the Old Trails Fire can request an asbestos survey at no cost.
  • Residential applicants for rebuilding permits can use a free application completeness screening from Permavia for one year, which is optional and does not replace the city's own review.
  • The city issued its first rebuild permit after the fires on August 28, 2026.
  • Spokane County publishes a Demolition and Rebuilding FAQ and a Next Steps FAQ for affected owners.
  • Call 311 inside the city, or 509.755.CITY (2489) from outside it, Monday through Friday from 7 a.m. to 6 p.m.

Owners who lost a house or hold a damaged one often weigh rebuilding against selling the lot or the shell. Ask your insurer in writing what a sale does to an open claim before you sign anything, and ask the county assessor how the damage changes your assessed value.

Which Spokane neighborhoods and schools shape what a house is worth?

The answer starts with where the house sits. Downtown and the Riverside neighborhood form the business center, the South Hill rises south of it, and Browne's Addition west of downtown is a National Historic District known for Queen Anne and Craftsman mansions. Hillyard in the northeast began in 1892 as the site of the Great Northern Railway yard. East Central, the University District and West Central round out the older core, and the city counts 18 National Register historic districts. If your home is in one, ask the city's planning staff whether exterior changes need design review before you repaint, re-side or replace windows for a sale.

Most of the city falls within Spokane Public Schools (District 81), the largest public district in the city. The Mead School District serves parts of north Spokane County outside city limits. Gonzaga University, founded in 1887, and Whitworth University, which moved to north Spokane in 1914, are the two best-known campuses in the city.

Jobs follow the same pattern. Education, health care and social assistance employ 26.5 percent of working residents, retail trade 12.7 percent, and the 92d Air Refueling Wing at Fairchild Air Force Base near Airway Heights is the largest military employer. Weather also reaches the house: Spokane averages about 16.5 inches of precipitation a year, 21 days at or above 90 degrees and roughly 2.2 days at or below zero, so roofs, furnaces and insulation get tested at both ends.

What permit steps and city rules come up before a Spokane sale?

Any repair that needed a permit should be closed out with the city before you list. Spokane runs permits through its Accela Citizen Access portal, and the Development Services Center keeps in-person hours of 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. on Monday, Tuesday, Thursday and Friday and 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. on Wednesday. The center is closed on November 26 and 27 for the holiday.

  • Pull permit history for work you did or inherited, such as a finished basement, a new deck or a water heater swap.
  • Ask the permit center how to resolve an open or expired permit before a buyer's inspector finds it.
  • Pay only through the city's portal. The city warns that fake permit invoices are circulating and says it never asks for payment through emailed wire instructions.

The county's parcel information search shows tax history and assessed value for any Spokane parcel, which helps you confirm the lot size and legal description that will go on the deed.

What taxes and paperwork apply when a Spokane house sells?

The seller normally pays Washington's real estate excise tax, and it is due to the county treasurer where the property sits on the date of sale, whether or not the deed has been recorded yet. For Spokane that means the Spokane County Treasurer. The state share is graduated: 1.1 percent on the first $525,000 of the price and 1.28 percent on the slice up to $1,525,000, with the thresholds rising to $551,000 and $1,551,000 for sales that start on January 1, 2027. A local share is added on top, so ask the treasurer for the exact combined rate before you set your net.

Tax not paid within one month of the sale collects interest, which the Department of Revenue lists at 6 percent for 2026. An unpaid tax can also become a lien on the property.

On most house sales you must hand the buyer a completed seller disclosure statement within five business days after both sides sign the purchase contract, and the buyer then has three business days to rescind unless the two of you agree otherwise (RCW 64.06.020). The form asks about structure, roof, systems, smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, and the buyer may waive receiving it. Read the statute and the Department of Revenue's excise tax page before closing.

When does a cash sale make sense for a Spokane house?

A cash sale fits when speed or condition matters more to you than the last few thousand dollars. A listing usually asks for repairs, showings and a financing timeline. A cash buyer takes the house in the shape it is in and can often close on a date you choose, which helps with a fire-damaged home, an inherited house or a rental with a problem tenant.

Before you accept any offer from a Spokane buyer, get these points in writing:

  • The purchase price and who pays the excise tax and recording costs.
  • The closing date and the title or escrow company that will handle it.
  • Whether the buyer will take the house with its repairs, its contents and any open permits.
  • How long the offer stays open and what happens to any earnest money.

Compare that offer with what a listing would net after repairs, commission and carrying costs. If the cash number is lower, the gap is the price of skipping the work and the wait.

More questions about Spokane, WA

How fast can I sell a house in Spokane?

The timeline depends on the route you pick. A cash purchase has no loan approval to wait for, so it can move faster than a listing, but title work and the escrow company set the real closing date.

Who pays the real estate excise tax on a Spokane sale?

The seller usually pays it. It is due to the Spokane County Treasurer on the date of sale, and the state portion is 1.1 percent on the first $525,000 of the price plus a local portion. Ask the treasurer for the combined rate.

Can I sell a fire-damaged house in Spokane?

Yes. Owners affected by the August 2026 Old Trails Fire can request a free asbestos survey from the city, and the county publishes demolition and rebuilding guidance. Talk to your insurer first about how a sale affects an open claim.

Do I have to give a Spokane buyer a seller disclosure statement?

Usually yes. Washington requires a completed form within five business days after the contract is signed on most residential sales, unless the buyer waives it or the transfer is exempt. The buyer then has three business days to rescind.

Where do I check property tax history for a Spokane house?

Use the Spokane County parcel information search, which lists tax history and assessed value. For a payoff or proration at closing, ask the Spokane County Treasurer.

What does the Tacoma housing market look like to a seller?

Tacoma homeowners report a median home value of $479,600 in the Census Bureau's 2020-2024 estimates, and 55.8 percent of households own rather than rent. The city is the county seat of Pierce County and the economic center of the South Sound region, with an estimated 229,816 residents on July 1, 2025.

Which Tacoma neighborhoods do buyers ask about?

Buyers tend to ask which part of town a house is in before anything else. The city is grouped into Central Tacoma, New Tacoma around downtown, North Tacoma, Northeast Tacoma, West Tacoma and the Port of Tacoma area, and each carries its own character.

  • Central Tacoma includes Hilltop, Delong Park, the Wedge, Bryant and College Heights.
  • North Tacoma includes the Proctor District, the North Slope, Old Tacoma, Ruston Way, Skyline and Yakima Hill.
  • West Tacoma includes the Highlands, Narrows, Titlow and Salmon Beach.
  • Downtown takes in the Stadium District, the Theater District, the Dome District and the Thea Foss Waterway.

Transit shapes demand around the core. Sound Transit runs the T Line between Tacoma Dome Station, downtown, the University of Washington Tacoma campus and Hilltop, and also operates Sounder trains and express buses toward Seattle. Most of the city belongs to Tacoma Public Schools, which lists 36 elementary schools, 11 middle schools and 10 high schools, including Stadium High School and Mount Tahoma High School. Ruston is a separately incorporated town and Browns Point is unincorporated, so confirm which jurisdiction your parcel sits in before you ask the City of Tacoma about permits. Tacoma also keeps a historic preservation program with 165 city landmarks and more than 1,000 historic properties across five overlay zones, so ask the city whether your older home sits in one before you plan exterior work.

How do Tacoma's land, water and climate affect a house?

Elevation and shoreline do most of the work. The city ranges from sea level to roughly 500 feet and covers 62.34 square miles, of which 12.62 square miles are water, and it wraps around Commencement Bay on Puget Sound. Many parts of the city have views of Mount Rainier, and the low-lying ground near the Port of Tacoma sits in the path of a lahar from the Puyallup River if the volcano ever erupts.

Tacoma has a warm-summer Mediterranean climate, with July and August the warmest months and December the coldest. Mean daily highs run 48.1 degrees in January and 76.9 in August. The industrial tide flats once produced the odor known as the Tacoma Aroma, which ended when the Simpson Tacoma Kraft mill closed in September 2023.

The Port of Tacoma is among the largest seaports in the Pacific Northwest, and a refinery has operated on the tide flats since 1952. Downtown has been revitalized since the 1990s, with the University of Washington Tacoma campus, the T Line and a restored Thea Foss Waterway. The Tacoma Narrows bridges connect the city to Gig Harbor and the Kitsap Peninsula.

What property maintenance changes are coming for Tacoma owners?

Tacoma adopted a new property maintenance standard that takes effect on January 1, 2027. The City Council passed Ordinance 29125, which brings International Property Maintenance Code standards into the city's Property Maintenance and Nuisance Code and strengthens the tools the city uses against repeat and chronic violations.

The city says it handles roughly 4,500 property maintenance cases a year under older rules in Chapters 8.30 and 2.01 of its code. Section 7 of the ordinance states that the expanded enforcement program becomes operational no earlier than nine months after the council funds it, so the day-to-day effect depends on future budget decisions. If you own a vacant, neglected or rental house in Tacoma, find out whether any open code complaint is attached to it, and read the details at tacoma.gov/IPMC. Ask the city for any open complaint on the property before you list.

What taxes and disclosures come with a Tacoma sale?

Pierce County bills and collects property tax for Tacoma addresses through the Assessor-Treasurer's office at 2401 S. 35th St., Room 142, in Tacoma, reachable at (253) 798-6111. The second-half 2026 payment deadline was November 2, so a closing now should settle any unpaid balance and prorate the part of the year that the buyer will own. Payments can be made online through the parcel search site, by phone at (253) 798-3333, by mail to Pierce County Finance, or at the cashier lobby at 1501 Market St., Suite 120, from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. on weekdays. Newer exemption rules also matter: starting in January 2027 more Pierce County homeowners who are 61 or older, or who have a qualifying disability, will see their taxes reduced under an expanded state program.

Real estate excise tax is due from the seller at the county treasurer on the date of sale. The state portion is 1.1 percent on the first $525,000 of the price and 1.28 percent on the amount between $525,000 and $1,525,000, and a local portion is added. Under RCW 64.06.020, a seller of most improved residential property must deliver a signed disclosure statement within five business days after the buyer and seller sign a contract. The form includes questions about the roof, plumbing, electrical and heating systems, and it notes that the seller must provide carbon monoxide alarms and at least one smoke detection device.

  • Gather your latest tax statement and any special assessments before listing.
  • Ask the county for the payoff amount on any unpaid taxes.
  • Collect permit records for additions, such as a converted garage or a new bathroom.
  • Check whether the city or the county has any open complaint or lien tied to the parcel.

Should I list my Tacoma house or take a cash offer?

The answer turns on your repair budget, your calendar and how much work the house needs before a buyer's inspector walks through. A listing exposes the house to the open market. A cash offer trades some of that exposure for speed and fewer conditions, which suits a vacant house, an inherited property or a rental with a tenant in place.

Whichever route you choose, compare written offers on net proceeds, not on the headline price. Ask each buyer who pays the excise tax, how long the offer is open, what the closing date is and whether they accept the house as it stands with its contents.

More questions about Tacoma, WA

Can I sell a house in Tacoma that needs repairs?

Yes. A cash buyer may purchase the house as it stands, and on most residential sales you must complete the seller disclosure statement describing the property's condition to the best of your knowledge.

What does Ordinance 29125 mean for Tacoma sellers?

It sets a new property maintenance standard that takes effect January 1, 2027. The expanded enforcement program starts no earlier than nine months after the council funds it, so check for open code complaints on your property before you sell.

Who collects property tax on a Tacoma house?

Pierce County does, through its Assessor-Treasurer's office in Tacoma. Call (253) 798-6111 for assessed values, statements and exemptions, and ask for a payoff figure before closing.

Who pays the excise tax when a Tacoma house sells?

The seller usually pays it, and it is due to the county treasurer on the date of sale. The state rate is graduated, starting at 1.1 percent on the first $525,000, with a local portion added.

How many people live in Tacoma?

The Census Bureau estimates 229,816 residents as of July 1, 2025, up from 219,346 at the April 2020 census. Tacoma is the third most populous city in Washington.

What should a seller know about Pasco, Washington?

Pasco is the county seat of Franklin County and one of the three Tri-Cities, with Kennewick and Richland across the Columbia River to the south. The Census Bureau estimates 82,848 residents as of July 1, 2025, up 7.1% from the April 2020 estimates base.

Pasco was incorporated on September 3, 1891, as a Northern Pacific Railway town. Grand Coulee Dam, completed in 1941, brought irrigation to the area and tied the city to farming for decades. The city covers about 34 square miles, roughly 30.5 of them land.

A seller here deals with city hall for permits and rental licenses, with the Franklin County Treasurer for tax and excise payments, and with the Pasco School District for school boundaries that buyers ask about. The rest of this page covers each in turn.

What do the Census numbers say about Pasco homes?

Seven in ten Pasco homes are owner-occupied. The table shows the main figures from Census QuickFacts.

MeasurePasco city

Source: U.S. Census Bureau QuickFacts. Households average 3.19 people, and the Census reports that 53.0% of residents age 5 and older speak a language other than English at home. If you or your buyer want signing help in another language, ask the closing office to arrange it early.

How does Pasco's desert climate affect a house sale?

Pasco sits in the rain shadow of the Cascade Range, so the area is dry and windy. Summers are hot, with a mean daily high of 93.3 degrees in July and a record high of 115 degrees in June, and winters are cold enough to reach a record low of minus 19 degrees in January.

Those swings put a premium on a few items a buyer will check:

  • Air conditioning age and capacity, since cooling runs for months.
  • Roof condition and attic insulation under strong summer sun.
  • Irrigation systems and landscaping that survive on little rain.
  • Pipes and exterior faucets that can freeze in a cold snap.

Service records for the cooling system and roof give a buyer something concrete to review. If a unit is near the end of its life, say so on the disclosure form rather than waiting for the inspector.

What do Pasco schools, jobs and neighborhoods mean for a seller?

The Pasco School District runs the city's public schools. Pasco High School is the older of two long-standing high schools, Chiawana High School opened in August 2009, and a third, Sageview High School, opened in 2025 to relieve crowding at Chiawana. Delta High School, a STEM program shared with the Kennewick and Richland districts, opened in 2015. Columbia Basin College and Washington State University Tri-Cities serve the city's students.

The Census shows 67.0% of residents age 16 and older in the labor force, and Census business data show about $359 million in 2022 transportation and warehousing receipts in Pasco. Mean travel time to work is 22.5 minutes. Buyers who commute across the river to Kennewick or Richland will weigh that against price.

Parts of Pasco are newer subdivisions and parts are older neighborhoods near downtown, so a nearby sale of a similar house is a better guide to price than the citywide median. Ask an agent or your cash buyer which recent sales they used.

Which Pasco city rules matter before you sell?

Pasco's Ordinance No. 4770, adopted June 2, 2025, removed permit requirements for several small jobs. The city's permit page lists them, and they matter if you want to tidy the house before listing:

  • One-story detached sheds or playhouses up to 200 square feet in residential areas.
  • Fences under 7 feet, retaining walls under 4 feet, and decks under 200 square feet and 30 inches high.
  • Residential roofing and siding replacement limited to the shingles, underlayment, flashing, siding, barrier and veneer.

Structural work, anything habitable, and building in an easement or too close to a property line still need a permit. A permit is good for 180 days from issue, and passing an inspection renews that clock, according to the city's ADU guide.

That guide, published in 2023, says Pasco allows one attached or detached ADU per residential parcel, up to 1,000 square feet or 55 percent of the main house, whichever is less. The unit must be long-term housing, with occupants living there more than 180 days a year, and short-term rentals are not allowed. Landlords need a rental business license under PMC 5.60.010. Call Pasco Community and Economic Development at (509) 545-3441 to confirm current rules for your zone.

How is real estate excise tax handled on a Pasco sale?

The seller owes it. RCW 82.45.080 makes the excise tax the seller's obligation. The state portion is 1.1% on the part of the price up to $525,000, then 1.28% to $1,525,000, then 2.75% to $3,025,000 and 3% above that, with the local portion added on top.

At the Census median of $376,300, the state portion alone would be about $4,139. The Department of Revenue moves the thresholds to $551,000, $1,551,000 and $3,051,000 for sales beginning January 1, 2027. Ask the Franklin County Treasurer for the local rate.

Payment is due on the date of sale, which is the date the deed is notarized, and the one-month grace period before interest starts runs from that date. You submit the affidavit, the deed and the payment to the county treasurer. If a seller overpays, a refund request must be filed within four years of the sale and the refund goes to the party who paid. The Department of Revenue REET page has the forms.

How do Franklin County property taxes work at closing?

Franklin County's Treasurer says taxes are payable on or after February 15, with the full amount due by April 30. When the bill is more than $50, half can be paid by April 30 and the second half by October 31. The Treasurer is at 1016 N 4th Avenue in Pasco, phone 509-545-3518.

For real property, the Treasurer starts foreclosure action when taxes have been delinquent for three years, so a seller with old arrears should pay them off at closing. Ask your closing officer for a current tax status before you sign.

Owners who are 61 or older, disabled, or disabled veterans may qualify for a deduction, and the Franklin County Assessor handles those applications at 509-545-3506. If you are selling because you can no longer keep up with the house, ask the Assessor whether a reduction would have applied in a prior year.

What options does a Pasco seller have?

A seller can list with an agent, sell without one, or accept an as-is offer from a cash buyer. Each ends with the same deed, affidavit and tax steps, so the choice comes down to timing, condition and price.

  • A listing suits a house in good shape and an owner who can wait through showings and financing.
  • A direct as-is sale suits a house with deferred repairs, a tenant, or an inherited property.
  • Ask any buyer who pays the excise tax, how the date of sale is set, and how back taxes are handled.

More questions about Pasco, WA

How much is the excise tax on a Pasco house sale?

It is 1.1% on the first $525,000 of the price under current state rules, plus a local portion set for Pasco. A $376,300 sale would owe about $4,139 at the state rate. The Franklin County Treasurer can quote the local rate.

When are Franklin County property taxes due?

The full tax is due by April 30, and for bills over $50 you may pay half by April 30 and the second half by October 31. The October 31, 2026 date has passed, so the next deadline is April 30, 2027.

Can I rent out an ADU in Pasco as a vacation rental?

No. The city's ADU guide says an ADU must be used for long-term residential purposes, with occupants living there more than 180 days a year, and short-term rentals are not allowed.

Do I need a permit to replace my roof in Pasco?

Not for a shingle, underlayment and flashing replacement. Ordinance 4770 removed that requirement, but structural roof work still needs a permit.

Who do I call about taxes for a senior or disabled owner in Franklin County?

The Franklin County Assessor at 509-545-3506. The county lists a deduction for owners who are 61 or older, disabled, or disabled veterans.

What should a seller know about Olympia, Washington?

Olympia is the capital of Washington and the county seat of Thurston County. The Census Bureau estimates 56,724 residents as of July 1, 2025, which is 2.4% above the April 2020 estimates base.

Olympia has a council-manager government and its own permit center at City Hall, 601 4th Avenue E. Most sellers deal with the city only if they have open permits, a rental, or a lot that could take more housing. The sections below cover those points, then the state and county steps every Olympia sale goes through.

How do Olympia's housing numbers compare?

Census QuickFacts gives a quick picture of who lives in Olympia and what homes are worth. The figures below come from the Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 survey period unless noted.

MeasureOlympia city
Population estimate, July 1, 202556,724
Owner-occupied housing unit rate49.8%
Median value of owner-occupied homes$486,200
Median gross rent$1,599
Households25,451
Persons per household2.16
Mean travel time to work20.0 minutes
Median household income$81,302

Source: U.S. Census Bureau QuickFacts. Under half of Olympia homes are owner-occupied, so many buyers and neighbors are renters or landlords. A median of $486,200 is a survey estimate across all owner-occupied homes, not a price for your house.

How does Olympia's weather affect a house for sale?

Olympia is wet, cloudy and mild. It averages about 50 inches of precipitation a year with roughly 75% cloud cover, and November through January are the rainiest months. City streets, creeks and rivers can flood between November and February.

Summer heat is rarer but real: the record high is 110 degrees, set on June 28, 2021, and an average of 6.3 days a year reach 90 degrees. Snow averages around 10.8 inches a season, though it has ranged from a trace to 81.5 inches in 1968 to 1969.

Buyers walking an Olympia house tend to look at the same few things:

  • Roof, gutters and downspouts, since the wet season runs for months.
  • Crawlspace and basement moisture, especially in older homes near the inlet or on fill.
  • Moss, rot and drainage around the foundation.
  • Cooling or ventilation, now that summers can reach the 90s and beyond.

Fixing or documenting these items before a showing shortens the inspection phase. A buyer taking the house as-is still reads the seller disclosure, so answer those questions accurately.

Which Olympia city rules matter when you sell?

Olympia allows up to two accessory dwelling units on almost all lots. Each can be up to 1,000 square feet and 24 feet tall, attached or detached. The city also allows middle housing in every residential zone: up to four units on a lot when zoning standards are met, and up to six within a half mile of frequent transit routes or when at least two units stay affordable for 50 years.

That flexibility can raise what a lot is worth to a builder or investor, so mention it if your lot is large. The city also offers six pre-approved ADU plans on its middle housing page.

Rental owners have a few extra steps. The state Department of Revenue's Olympia endorsement page says the city may require rental registration and, for short-term vacation rentals, an additional permit, both filed through the city's online permit portal. A general city business license costs $30 when reported gross income is above $4,000.

  • Permit Center: City Hall, second floor, 601 4th Avenue E, phone 360.753.8314.
  • Counter hours: Monday to Thursday, 9 a.m. to 4 p.m., closed Fridays.
  • Inspections and permit status are handled through the city's online permit portal.

If an old project never got a final inspection, call the Permit Center before you list and ask what the permit record shows.

How much real estate excise tax does an Olympia seller pay?

The seller owes Washington's real estate excise tax, plus any local portion set for the city. RCW 82.45.080 makes the tax the seller's obligation. The state portion is graduated: 1.1% on the part of the price up to $525,000, 1.28% on the part from $525,000 to $1,525,000, 2.75% up to $3,025,000, and 3% above that.

The Department of Revenue lists new thresholds for sales beginning January 1, 2027: $551,000, $1,551,000 and $3,051,000. At the Census median of $486,200, the state portion would be 1.1%, or about $5,348, before the local rate. Ask the Thurston County Treasurer for the local rate that applies to your address.

The tax is due on the date of sale, which the Department of Revenue defines as the date the deed is notarized, whether or not the deed is recorded that day. If the tax is not paid within one month of the sale date, interest applies. The affidavit, deed and payment go to the county treasurer where the property sits. More detail is on the Department of Revenue REET page.

How do Thurston County property taxes work at closing?

Thurston County bills property tax in two halves. The first half is due April 30 and the balance is due October 31, and a due date that lands on a weekend moves to the following Monday. In 2026 the second-half date fell on a Saturday, so it moved to Monday, November 2, which has now passed.

Taxes follow the property, not the owner, and the county does not send new statements when a house changes hands. The Treasurer's FAQ says it is your responsibility to decide how taxes are handled in your closing and to know whether the property still has taxes due for the year. Ask your closing agent to prorate the current year and to pay any unpaid half from sale proceeds.

Sellers who are 61 or older, or retired from a disability, may have a tax reduction or a deferral. Those programs run through the Thurston County Assessor, at 360-867-2200 per the Treasurer's FAQ. A deferral is repaid from the estate, so confirm the payoff with the county before closing.

  • Treasurer's office: 3000 Pacific Avenue SE, Suite 130, Olympia, phone 360-786-5550.
  • Special charges such as stormwater can appear on the same bill and are liens too.
  • Real property is not sold for unpaid tax until three full years of delinquency.

What does an Olympia seller have to hand the buyer?

For a sale of improved residential property, the seller must deliver a completed disclosure statement, unless the buyer waives it or the transfer is exempt. RCW 64.06.020 sets the form and says delivery must happen within five business days of a mutual acceptance unless the parties agree otherwise.

The buyer then has three business days after delivery to rescind. If you do not provide the statement, the buyer may instead waive the right to rescind before or after the contract. Complete every line, write NA where a question does not apply, and explain any yes answer on an attached sheet.

Disclosure covers what you actually know. Past roof leaks, drainage problems and permit history in an older Olympia house all belong on the form if you know of them.

What are the ways to sell a house in Olympia?

Most Olympia owners choose among three routes, and the same deed, excise tax and tax proration steps apply to each.

  • List with a real estate agent and accept the time showings, repairs and buyer financing take.
  • Sell on your own, which means handling the disclosure form, the contract and the closing paperwork yourself.
  • Take an as-is offer from a cash buyer, which can cut repairs and financing delays, though the price usually sits below a fully prepared listing.

Compare written offers, ask what each buyer expects you to pay at closing, and keep the deed and affidavit timing in mind so the sale date and tax payment line up.

More questions about Olympia, WA

How much is the excise tax when I sell a house in Olympia?

It depends on the price and the local rate. The state portion is 1.1% on the first $525,000 of the sale, 1.28% on the next slice up to $1,525,000, and higher above that, with new thresholds starting January 1, 2027. The Thurston County Treasurer can tell you the local rate for your address.

When are Thurston County property taxes due?

The first half is due April 30 and the second half is due October 31, with weekend dates moving to the next Monday. The 2026 second-half deadline was Monday, November 2, so it has passed. The next first-half deadline is April 30, 2027.

Can I build an extra unit on my Olympia lot before selling?

Often yes. Olympia allows up to two ADUs on almost all lots, each up to 1,000 square feet and 24 feet tall, and middle housing of up to four units in residential zones when standards are met. Call the Permit Center at 360.753.8314 to check your lot before you start.

Who pays the real estate excise tax in Washington, buyer or seller?

The seller. RCW 82.45.080 makes it the seller's obligation, though the buyer can become responsible if the seller does not pay, and unpaid tax can become a lien on the property.

Where do I file the excise tax affidavit for an Olympia house?

With the Thurston County Treasurer, together with the deed and payment, because the tax is paid to the treasurer of the county where the property sits. Your closing or escrow officer normally handles this at signing.

What should a seller know about Puyallup, Washington?

Puyallup is a Pierce County city on the Puyallup River, about 10 miles southeast of Tacoma and 35 miles south of Seattle. The Census Bureau estimates 42,682 residents as of July 1, 2025, a 0.7% dip from the April 2020 estimates base.

Ezra Meeker platted the townsite in 1877, and his hop farm drove growth through the 1880s until the town incorporated in 1890. Today the city is best known for the Washington State Fair, the state's largest annual fair. The city covers about 14 square miles of valley floor.

One detail trips up many sellers. Mailing addresses that say Puyallup also cover unincorporated areas such as South Hill, so check whether your parcel is inside city limits. That decides which permit office, zoning code and utility rules apply, while the county bills property tax either way.

What do the Census numbers say about Puyallup homes?

The Census puts Puyallup's median home value above $550,000 and its average commute above half an hour. The table collects the main QuickFacts figures.

MeasurePuyallup city
Population estimate, July 1, 202542,682
Owner-occupied housing unit rate, 2020 to 202452.1%
Median value of owner-occupied homes$551,800
Median gross rent$1,812
Households16,570
Persons per household2.53

Source: U.S. Census Bureau QuickFacts. A 31.4-minute mean commute means many buyers will weigh drive time to Tacoma, Seattle and other job centers. The median home value is a survey estimate across all owner-occupied homes, so a recently updated house can price well above it.

How does Mount Rainier's lahar zone affect a Puyallup house?

Downtown Puyallup and nearby neighborhoods lie within a hazard zone for lahars, which are mudflows that a moderate or large Mount Rainier eruption could send down the Puyallup Valley. The city's rules respond to that risk. Under Puyallup Municipal Code 20.20.010(11)(L), accessory dwelling units are prohibited in the lahar exclusion area, with an exception for land within a half mile of the base of the surrounding elevation of the valley floor.

The city's September 2025 tip sheet explains what owners in that area can still do:

  • Build an addition or remodel that has an internal doorway and is not fully fire-wall separated from the main home.
  • Rent that added space to family or, if not family, to no more than one person.
  • Keep a guest house in a detached building, as long as it has no independent cooking facilities and no one lives there full time, with limited exceptions for family and employees.

If your house has a converted garage, a basement apartment or a backyard cottage, confirm with the Planning Division how the city treats it before you list. An unpermitted second unit can complicate a sale. Call 253-864-4165, option 3, or email Planning@PuyallupWA.gov.

What do Puyallup schools, roads and permits look like for a seller?

The Puyallup School District has 35 schools and serves more than 22,534 students, making it the ninth-largest district in the state. Its boundaries extend beyond the city to South Hill, parts of Tacoma and the Edgewood area. Pierce College Puyallup is a community college in the city.

State Routes 167 and 512 meet at Puyallup, giving freeway access toward Lakewood and the Green River Valley. Sounder commuter trains stop at Puyallup station on weekdays, and Pierce Transit buses and a microtransit zone that launched in 2023 serve the city.

The city Permit Center is on the second floor of City Hall at 333 South Meridian, with counter hours of 9 a.m. to 3 p.m., and the main line is 253-864-4165. Anyone with an open building permit should ask the center to confirm its status.

How much real estate excise tax does a Puyallup seller owe?

The seller pays it under RCW 82.45.080, and the state portion is graduated. Through December 31, 2026, the rates are 1.1% up to $525,000, 1.28% from $525,000 to $1,525,000, 2.75% to $3,025,000 and 3% above. A local portion is added on top, which the Pierce County Assessor-Treasurer can quote for your address.

For sales beginning January 1, 2027, the Department of Revenue moves the thresholds to $551,000, $1,551,000 and $3,051,000. The Census median home value of $551,800 sits right at that new line. At that price, the state portion works out to about $6,118 under the 2026 brackets and about $6,071 under the 2027 brackets, a difference of roughly $47.

The sale date for tax purposes is the date the deed is notarized, not the recording date. The affidavit, deed and payment go to the county treasurer. After a payment, a refund request must be filed within four years of the sale and goes to the party who paid. See the Department of Revenue REET page.

How do Pierce County property taxes work at closing?

The first half of property tax is due April 30 and the second half by October 31. The county's FAQ says that because October 31 fell on a weekend in 2026, the second half was due Monday, November 2, a date that has now passed. A bill of $50 or less is due in full by April 30.

For residential property with one to four units, interest of 0.75% per month is charged on the full year's tax beginning May 1 if the first half is late, for tax year 2023 and later. You can still pay the first half plus interest through October 31. Ask your closing officer to settle any late amount from sale proceeds.

Pierce County values property at 100% of market value every year and physically inspects each property about once every six years. An owner who disagrees with the value may appeal to the Board of Equalization by July 1 of the assessment year or within 60 days of a value change notice, whichever is later. Only market value can be argued, not the size of the tax bill.

Seniors and people with disabilities may qualify for a property tax deferral. The state pays the tax, and the deferred amount becomes a lien that must be repaid with interest when ownership transfers, under RCW 84.38. If you hold a deferral, request a payoff figure early. The Assessor-Treasurer is at 2401 South 35th Street, Room 142, Tacoma, phone 253-798-6111.

What are the ways to sell a house in Puyallup?

A Puyallup owner can list the house, sell without an agent, or accept an as-is offer from a cash buyer. All three end with the same deed, excise tax affidavit and tax proration at closing.

  • A listing can reach the widest pool of buyers, with the time that showings and financing require.
  • An as-is offer suits a house with deferred repairs, an unpermitted unit or a conversion in the lahar zone.
  • Ask any buyer what they will pay for, who covers the excise tax, and when they want the deed notarized.

More questions about Puyallup, WA

Can I build a backyard cottage in Puyallup's lahar zone?

No. Puyallup Municipal Code 20.20.010(11)(L) prohibits accessory dwelling units in the lahar exclusion area, with an exception near the edge of the valley floor. A guest house with no independent cooking, not lived in full time, may be allowed.

When is the second half of Pierce County property tax due?

October 31, or the next business day if that date falls on a weekend. In 2026 it was Monday, November 2, which has passed. The next first-half date is April 30, 2027.

How much is the excise tax on a $551,800 Puyallup sale?

About $6,118 in state tax under the 2026 brackets, or about $6,071 if the sale takes place on or after January 1, 2027, before the local portion is added. The date the deed is notarized decides which brackets apply.

Does a South Hill address mean my house is in the city of Puyallup?

Not always. Puyallup mailing addresses cover adjacent unincorporated areas such as South Hill. Check your parcel with the city Planning Division or the county to confirm which rules apply.

What happens to a senior property tax deferral when I sell?

The amount the state paid on your behalf becomes a lien that is repaid, with interest, when ownership transfers. Request a payoff figure from the Pierce County Assessor-Treasurer before closing.

Where is University Place, and how did the city take shape?

University Place is a mostly suburban city in Pierce County on the west side of Tacoma, with waterfront on Puget Sound. It covers 8.34 square miles of land, sits at about 417 feet of elevation, and is bordered by Puget Sound to the west, Lakewood to the south, and Tacoma to the north and east, with Fircrest along part of the eastern edge.

The name goes back to the 1800s, when the University of Puget Sound bought land along Grandview Drive for a campus. The school ended up selling the land back for about $11,000. The area stayed unincorporated until the City of University Place was formed on August 31, 1995.

Chambers Bay is the best-known landmark. The links-style golf course opened in 2007 and hosted the 2010 U.S. Amateur and the 2015 U.S. Open. The 28-acre University Place Town Center, built in the late 2000s and early 2010s, holds the city hall, a Pierce County Library branch, the police offices, a public plaza and a mix of homes and shops. The Village at Chambers Bay has metered parking on Market Place, and the city runs parking enforcement patrols there. Cirque Park hosts community events and youth sports programs run with the Pearl Street YMCA, and the city invited residents to a Veterans Day celebration at Veterans Plaza in the park. University Place uses a council-manager form of government, with a seven-member council led by Mayor Stan Flemming.

Which public schools serve homes in University Place?

The University Place School District serves most of the city and runs eight public schools. Primary schools teach kindergarten through fourth grade, intermediate schools cover grades five through seven, junior high is grades eight and nine, and high school is grades ten through twelve.

  • Primary: Chambers, Evergreen, Sunset and University Place.
  • Intermediate: Drum and Narrows View.
  • Junior high and high school: Curtis Junior High and Curtis Senior High.

The city requires a permit any time you construct, enlarge, alter, repair, move or demolish a building, or change its occupancy, and also for installing or replacing electrical, gas, mechanical or plumbing systems. Before listing, ask the department whether any finished work, such as a converted garage, a new furnace or a water heater swap, is missing a final inspection, and keep the paper trail for the buyer.

  • Work along 67th Avenue West from 40th Street West to Regents Boulevard West, adding sidewalks, landscaping and lighting, was set to begin on October 26.
  • Repair and resurfacing of Cirque Drive West from 67th Avenue West to Orchard Street was scheduled to begin September 14.
  • Grandview Senior Living is under construction at Grandview Drive West and 27th Street West.

The city also reminds residents that raked leaves belong in yard waste bags, not in the street, where they can clog storm drains and gutters.

What does real estate excise tax cost on a University Place sale?

The city's own tax page says its share of the real estate excise tax is 0.5 percent of the price, collected with the state's portion by the Pierce County Treasurer. The county keeps 1 percent of what it collects for collection costs and sends the other 99 percent to the city each month, where it may be used to finance capital projects. A sale at the $624,800 median value crosses the first state bracket, so the combined cost is a blend of rates rather than one flat figure. Ask a title company for the exact calculation.

Starting in January 2027, more Pierce County homeowners who are 61 or older, or who have a qualifying disability, will see their property taxes reduced under an expanded state program.

Washington's seller disclosure law, RCW 64.06.020, gives the buyer three business days after delivery of the form to rescind the agreement unless both sides agree otherwise. If the seller does not hand over a completed form, the buyer may waive that right before or after signing the contract.

Listing makes sense when the house is in good shape and you can wait for showings and a buyer's financing. A cash offer fits better when the house needs repairs, belongs to an estate, or has to close on a set date.

  • Confirm the closing date and who handles escrow.
  • Get the offer in writing, with its expiration date.

If you inherited the house, ask a probate attorney or the Pierce County Superior Court what authority you need before anyone can sign a deed.

What should a seller know about Pullman, Washington?

Pullman is a college town in the Palouse, in the eastern part of Whitman County about 65 miles south of Spokane and 32 miles north of Lewiston, Idaho. The Census Bureau estimates 33,756 residents as of July 1, 2025, which is 2.6% above the April 2020 estimates base. Washington State University, the state's land-grant college, is the reason most buyers and renters come.

Settlers staked claims on the site in the 1870s, and the town was incorporated on April 11, 1888. The legislature created the land-grant college in 1890, and Pullman leaders offered 160 acres to win it. The city covers about 11 square miles, all of it land.

Selling here usually means thinking about two kinds of buyer: families who want to stay and investors who want a student rental. The city's rental registration and short-term rental rules, covered below, apply to the second group.

What rental rules apply to a Pullman house?

Owners of residential rental property must register with the City of Pullman under Pullman City Code 6.98. The Police Department's permits and licenses page lists a one-time registration fee of $15 per address and names the Code Enforcement Supervisor, at 509-334-0802, for questions.

Short-term rentals are a separate process under Pullman City Code chapter 17.109. The city's application instructions list what an owner submits:

  • A business license using NAICS code 721199, applied for before final approval.
  • Insurance and liability coverage as required by RCW 64.37.050.
  • A floor plan showing beds, smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, fire extinguishers and an emergency egress light.
  • An evacuation plan and a plot plan showing off-street parking.
  • A $200 short-term rental fee, paid before review starts.

Approval can carry an occupancy limit of the number of sleeping rooms plus two. If your house runs as a rental, tell a buyer which registrations are current and hand over the paperwork.

How do Pullman's hills and weather affect a house?

Pullman sits across four hills of windblown loess: Military Hill, Pioneer Hill, Sunnyside Hill and College Hill. Elevation runs from about 2,342 to 2,575 feet, and downtown lies in a valley where Missouri Flat Creek and Paradise Creek join the South Fork of the Palouse River. Steep lots and drainage are worth documenting if your house sits on a slope.

Winters are cold and wet and summers are hot and dry. The city's building division publishes design criteria that give a sense of what houses must handle: a ground snow load of 30 pounds per square foot, a frost depth of 30 inches, energy code climate zone 5B, and a required ice barrier underlayment on roofs.

Pullman adopted the 2021 International Building and Residential Codes, effective March 15, 2024. Reroofing, residing and replacement windows often need no plan review, and the city can issue those permits online, over the counter or next day. Projects that change the structure or footprint go through plan review that can take four to six weeks.

Applications can be emailed to pwcd-admin@pullman-wa.gov, and the office is at 190 SE Crestview Street, Building A. Finish any open permit before you list, because a buyer's lender or inspector may ask about it.

Which schools and roads serve Pullman buyers?

The Pullman School District covers Franklin, Jefferson, Sunnyside and Kamiak elementary schools, Lincoln Middle School and Pullman High School, the city's only public high school. Pullman High is on Military Hill, and students can take Running Start courses through WSU and Spokane Falls Community College.

U.S. Route 195 and State Route 27 run north toward Spokane and the Palouse towns, US 195 also runs south to Lewiston, and State Route 270 connects Pullman with Moscow, Idaho. Pullman Transit serves residents and WSU students. The Census puts mean travel time to work at 14.6 minutes.

If your house is close to campus or a bus line, say so in the listing, since a 14.6-minute average commute is part of what makes the location attractive.

How much real estate excise tax does a Pullman seller owe?

The seller owes it. RCW 82.45.080 puts the excise tax on the seller, and the state portion is graduated: 1.1% up to $525,000, 1.28% from there to $1,525,000, 2.75% to $3,025,000 and 3% above. A local portion is added, so ask the Whitman County Treasurer which rate applies in the city.

At the Census median of $424,800, the state portion would be about $4,673. For sales beginning January 1, 2027, the Department of Revenue raises the thresholds to $551,000, $1,551,000 and $3,051,000. The date that counts is the date the deed is notarized, so a closing signed in late December uses the 2026 thresholds.

The Whitman County Treasurer lists real estate excise tax among its duties, so the affidavit, deed and payment go to its office at 400 N Main Street in Colfax. Unpaid tax can create a lien on the property, and the buyer can become responsible if the seller does not pay.

How do Whitman County property taxes work at closing?

State law, RCW 84.56.020, sets April 30 and October 31 as the two payment dates, and a bill of $50 or less is due in full by April 30. Whitman County's treasurer page carries a notice that property taxes are due by October 31. Ask the Treasurer which schedule your parcel follows.

  • Treasurer: 400 N Main Street, Colfax, mailing address P.O. Box 550, phone 509-397-6230.
  • Office hours listed on the county site: 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.
  • Ask your closing officer to prorate the year and clear any unpaid half from sale proceeds.

Ask the Whitman County Assessor whether a senior, disability or other reduction applies to your parcel. If you are behind on taxes, call the Treasurer before you list. The Treasurer's page announced a tax foreclosure sale for November 7 to 10, 2025.

What are the ways to sell a house in Pullman?

A Pullman owner can list the house, sell directly, or take an as-is offer from a cash buyer. The deed and excise tax steps are the same either way.

  • Listing works best when timing lines up with the academic calendar and the house shows well.
  • A direct sale to an investor can fit a rental with tenants, deferred repairs or a lease that ends mid-year.
  • Ask each buyer how they handle tenant notice, registration records and the closing date.

What is the owner-occupied rate in Pullman?

The Census reports 32.0% for 2020 to 2024, meaning roughly two of every three occupied homes are rented. Expect many buyers to be investors or to ask about rental history.

Do I have to register a rental house in Pullman?

Yes. Pullman City Code 6.98 requires owners of residential rental property to register with the city, with a one-time $15 fee per address, according to the Police Department's licensing page.

What does a short-term rental permit cost in Pullman?

The city's application instructions list a $200 short-term rental fee, paid before review begins. You also need a business license under NAICS code 721199 and the insurance that RCW 64.37.050 requires.

How long does a Pullman building permit take?

Reroofing, residing and window replacement may be issued online, over the counter or next day. More involved projects take four to six weeks for plan review.

Who collects the excise tax when a Pullman house sells?

The Whitman County Treasurer in Colfax, because the tax is paid to the county where the property sits. The seller owes it under RCW 82.45.080.

Tumwater lies in Thurston County about two miles south of Olympia, near the spot where the Deschutes River drops into Budd Inlet at the southern tip of Puget Sound. The city calls itself the end of the Oregon Trail and the oldest permanent American settlement on Puget Sound.

Michael T. Simmons led the first American settlers to Tumwater Falls in 1845, and the settlement was first called New Market before it took the Chinook jargon name for a waterfall by 1863. Tumwater was incorporated as a town on November 25, 1869. The falls powered early sawmills along the river, and the city's history pages still feature the old brewhouse and several historic houses. The Tumwater Historic District, listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1978, preserves what remained of downtown after Interstate 5 opened in 1958 and required the demolition of about 100 buildings.

The 1845 party also included George Bush, whose family settled on the prairies to the south, and the group cut the wagon trail that became the northern branch of the Oregon Trail. If your house is old or sits near the falls, ask the city's Community Development Department at (360) 754-4180 whether any local historic listing or critical area rule touches the lot.

What jobs and schools support demand in Tumwater?

Employers shape who shops for a house here. The city's economic profile, drawn from Thurston County economic development research, lists major employers that include:

  • Home Depot with 341 employees and Fred Meyer with 319.
  • Dart Container with 233, Amcor Rigid Packaging with 150 and Pepsi Northwest Beverages with 140.
  • Cardinal Glass Industries with 100 and Valmet with 94.

The Tumwater School District serves the city, and its high schools include Tumwater High School and Black Hills High School. The city's profile points to the state's school report card for district results. Mean commute time to work is 21.3 minutes, according to the Census Bureau.

The profile's 2022 age table shows 20.9 percent of residents under 18, 18.6 percent aged 25 to 34 and 16.1 percent aged 35 to 44. The same profile counts 27,100 people inside city limits in 2023 and another 2,890 in the urban growth area, for a total of 29,990. Tumwater Square, northeast of the old downtown, remains a local shopping center.

What building and permit rules apply to a Tumwater house?

The City of Tumwater's Community Development Department, through its Building Division, regulates construction, renovations and new building under the Tumwater Municipal Code. The division also conducts building and fire code plan reviews and inspections, and the city has a Development Review Committee that helps decide whether a project is feasible.

Before listing, work through these steps:

  • Pull permit records for any addition, deck, finished basement or mechanical replacement made since you bought.
  • Ask the Building Division how to close an open permit, and call (360) 754-4180 for platting and planned unit development questions.
  • Check zoning, which the city publishes alongside its building codes and development guide.
  • Look at the city's Development Projects interactive map to see which public and private projects are underway near your street.

The city is also asking residents to mark an interactive map of places where more attention is needed for climate resilience planning. In October 2026 Thurston County also urged residents to prepare for fall and winter flooding from major rivers, heavy rain, saturated soils, rising groundwater and overwhelmed drainage systems. If your lot is near the river or a low area, ask the city what the map shows and whether any flood or drainage rule affects the property.

What tax and paperwork steps come with selling in Tumwater?

Thurston County's Treasurer collects property tax for Tumwater parcels from an office at 3000 Pacific Ave SE in Olympia, open Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., and can be reached at 360-786-5550. The first half of the 2026 property tax was due April 30, and the second half was due October 31, with taxpayers given until Monday, November 2 because the 31st fell on a Saturday. Taxes can be paid online, in person, in the drop box in front of the building or by mail, and the county advises mailing early because the post office no longer guarantees same-day postmarks. Both deadlines have passed, so ask the treasurer whether any balance remains before closing.

Real estate excise tax is a separate bill. The seller normally pays it to the county treasurer where the property sits, it is due on the date of sale, and it becomes a lien on the property if nobody pays. State rates start at 1.1 percent on the first $525,000 of the price, move to 1.28 percent up to $1,525,000, and add a local portion. Interest accrues once a month passes without payment.

The seller disclosure statement under RCW 64.06.020 covers the roof, foundation, plumbing, electrical system, heating, drainage and more. It must reach the buyer within five business days after the contract is signed on most home sales, and it notes that a seller must provide carbon monoxide alarms and at least one smoke detection device. The statute has the full form.

Is a cash offer a reasonable way to sell a Tumwater house?

It can be, especially when the house needs work or the calendar is tight. A cash buyer in Tumwater takes the house as it stands and has no loan approval to wait for, so the sale does not depend on a lender's appraisal or a repair list.

Weigh these points against a traditional listing:

  • Net proceeds after commission, repairs and carrying costs compared with the cash price.
  • The closing date and whether it matches your move.
  • Who covers the excise tax, title and recording fees.
  • How the buyer treats an open permit, a tenant or items left in the house.

Get any Tumwater offer in writing, and ask a title or escrow company in Thurston County to confirm the payoff and the deed process before you sign.

More questions about Tumwater, WA

How many people live in Tumwater?

The Census Bureau estimates 28,010 residents as of July 1, 2025, up from 25,350 at the April 2020 census and 17,371 in 2010.

Which county handles property tax in Tumwater?

Thurston County does. The Treasurer's office is at 3000 Pacific Ave SE in Olympia and can be reached at 360-786-5550. The 2026 second-half deadline has passed, so ask about any balance before closing.

Who pays real estate excise tax when a Tumwater house sells?

The seller usually pays it to the county treasurer on the date of sale. The state portion starts at 1.1 percent on the first $525,000 and a local portion is added. If it goes unpaid it can become a lien on the property.

Do I need permits closed before selling a Tumwater house?

It is a good idea. Contact the Community Development Department's Building Division at (360) 754-4180 about permits for additions or major systems, and keep the records for the buyer.

What is Tumwater known for?

The city describes itself as the oldest permanent American settlement on Puget Sound and the end of the Oregon Trail. It sits at Tumwater Falls, where the Deschutes River meets Budd Inlet, and it was incorporated in 1869. The climate is a very warm-summer Mediterranean type, with warm, dry summers.
